title: vim on Linux replaces the document's identity and keeps the old one as a backup — where the same vim on darwin kept it

provenance.evidence: Four readings. `.doc.txt.swp` appears at inode 550185. `doc.txt` KEEPS ITS NAME AND CHANGES INODE, 550184 -> 550186, at size 6. `doc.txt~` then appears AT THE OLD INODE 550184 carrying the original 23 bytes. The swap file vanishes. The document is never seen at length zero, because it is never truncated: a new object is written and the old one is renamed aside. Captured by tests/compatibility/save-patterns/v0/capture.mjs, same command and same vim 9.0 major as the darwin capture.
blind_spots: open, flush, fsync and close are invisible to polling
polling cannot order the rename of the original against the creation of the replacement when both land inside one reading

objects.role: the ORIGINAL doc.txt at inode 550184 — renamed aside to doc.txt~, never truncated
the REPLACEMENT doc.txt at inode 550186 — a different object under the same name

folder.fidelity: a backend that does not declare ObserveDurableBoundary
folder.omission_note: No omission is declared admissible. Every reading in this capture carried a distinct object, so a dropped reading loses an object rather than merging two views of one — which is a different pattern, not this one seen imperfectly.

expected.meaningful_durable_change: doc.txt holds `short`. One durable change for one editor save — but the object carrying it is NOT the object the workspace held before, and doc.txt~ is a real new file the person now has.
expected.forbidden_note: Mount 3 is the moment the original has been renamed aside and the replacement does not exist yet: a checkpoint there records a workspace whose document has VANISHED and whose only trace is a backup file. That is the hazard this pattern contributes, and it is the mirror image of the darwin hazard — there the danger is a file momentarily EMPTY, here it is a file momentarily ABSENT. The checkpoint runs through 7 while its boundary evidence stops at 6: the window closes on settling after the swap file is unlinked, but the last thing the backend could PROVE was the replacement closing.

notes: THE CROSS-PLATFORM DIVERGENCE. The darwin capture of this same command, at the same vim major version, produced vim-in-place-truncate: ONE inode going 23 -> 0 -> 6, no backup file in the tree. Linux produced a rename-aside and a fresh object. Same tool, same flags, opposite object-identity semantics.

This falsifies any coalescing rule inferred from the darwin corpus alone. 01KZC2YXH6FG9C67JP9DQX7JH6's line 'never coalesce across a rename that changes object identity' does not fire at all on darwin vim and fires on every Linux vim save — so a rule validated only on darwin would look correct while never having been exercised.

It also means `doc.txt~` is a durable artifact of an ordinary save. A workspace that captures it presents the person a file they did not create; one that filters it is filtering by name, which is a heuristic and must be declared as one.
